unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 9, the final unit of Year 8. This unit is called "Music as Universal Language" because you will explore how music, performance, and the creative arts bring people together across cultures, languages, and backgrounds. Music is one of the most powerful forms of human expression. It can communicate emotions that words alone cannot capture. A song can make you feel joy, sorrow, excitement, or peace without you understanding a single word of the language in which it is sung. That is why we call music a universal language: it speaks to everyone.
unit.learningPath: Preview the goals and vocabulary. Read and annotate the source texts. Compare evidence, viewpoint and source reliability. Apply the grammar focus. Draft and revise a cohesive multi-paragraph response. Present, defend, reflect and complete the quiz.

readings.title: What Makes Music a Universal Language?
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Walk through any market in Kampala on a busy morning and listen. A radio crackles out a familiar chorus, a stallholder hums along, and two children clap a rhythm against a wooden crate. Nobody planned this soundtrack, and nobody needs it explained. Music slips past the barriers that separate people and speaks directly to feeling, which is why so many writers call it a universal language.
The claim is easy to test. A lullaby calms a baby who understands no words at all, because the melody itself carries the comfort. A stadium chant unites thousands of strangers who may share no mother tongue, yet they rise and fall together on the same beat. A film score can make an audience anxious before anything frightening appears on the screen. In each case the message arrives without translation, carried by rhythm, pitch and tone rather than by vocabulary.
Even the history of the word points the same way. 'Music' comes from the ancient Greek word 'mousike', meaning 'art of the Muses', the famous figures of inspiration in Greek mythology. The Arabic word for music, 'musiqa', grew from the same root, so communities separated by geography and language still reach for cousins of one ancient term. Many cultures have treasured music and poetry as precious gifts to be handled with care, and that respect survives today in how seriously performers train.
Performance turns this shared language into conversation. When musicians from different traditions play together, they trade phrases the way speakers trade sentences. A drummer states an idea, a violinist answers, and the audience follows the exchange without needing a word of explanation. Dancers hold the same kind of conversation with movement, and actors with gesture and expression. Watch a skilled mime for two minutes and you will apprehend an entire story, though the performer never speaks.
That is also why honest performance matters so much. Because music and theatre communicate feeling directly, a dishonest performance is not just weak art; it is a false message delivered in the most persuasive language human beings possess. A singer who fakes emotion, or a team that wins applause through sabotage rather than skill, sullies something the whole audience shares. The most formidable performers are usually the most truthful ones, because audiences sense sincerity the way they sense rhythm: instantly, and without being told.
In this unit you will read 'The Curtain Never Lies'. It is a story about a school drama team whose belief in honest art is tested on the biggest stage of their lives. You will meet vocabulary that describes skill, character and change, from 'deft' and 'muster' to 'vulnerable' and 'materialize'. You will practise the Present Perfect Continuous, the tense English uses when the length of an effort matters: 'They have been rehearsing since Monday.' You will also learn to shape participle clauses, exclamations and polite questions, the small structures that let you respond to art with precision.
Keep one question in mind as you work through these pages. What do you want your own performances, your words, your writing and your music, to do to the people who receive them? By the end of the unit you should be able to argue, in clear and confident English, that music is a universal language. You should also be able to explain exactly what that honest, wordless language is for.

readings.title: Behind the Curtain: How a School Production Comes Together
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
An audience sees two hours of polished performance. What it rarely sees is the months of unglamorous work that made those hours possible. Understanding that hidden work will change how you watch any play or concert, and it will make you a far sharper reviewer.
Every production begins with a script and a director. The director reads the script until she can see it: who stands where, what the light does, which silences matter. She then plans the blocking, the map of every actor's movement across the stage. Early rehearsals are slow and repetitive. Actors read their lines flat, forget them, and read them again. A director who wants honest performances does not demand perfection at this stage; she asks questions instead. Why does your character say this? What has she been doing all day before this scene? Actors who can answer such questions stop reciting and start becoming.
While the cast rehearses, a second team works in parallel. Designers sketch costumes and build props, choosing carefully between the striking and the gaudy. A prop is never just an object; a torn letter, a wooden mask or a strange concoction in a painted bottle can carry a whole scene's meaning. Technicians rig the lights and time the sound cues, because a thunderclap that arrives two seconds late can render a serious moment comic. Stage managers write everything into a master book: every entrance, every cue, every costume change, timed to the second.
The final week belongs to the dress rehearsal, the first complete run with full costume, light and sound. Directors expect it to meander and stall; its purpose is to let mistakes materialize now, while they are still free. A dropped line in an empty theatre costs nothing. The same mistake on opening night, in front of six hundred people, costs confidence. Good teams treat the dress rehearsal the way a scientist treats an experiment: every failure is information, recorded accurately and fixed the next day.
Then the audience arrives, and a new craft begins: judging what they see. A useful performance review does four things. It describes what actually happened on stage, briefly and precisely, so that a reader who was absent can picture it. It praises specific strengths with evidence: not 'the acting was good' but 'the lead's trembling hands made the confession scene painful to watch'. It criticises constructively, naming what was unclear or uneven and suggesting what might improve it. Finally, it weighs both sides and gives a fair recommendation. A review that only flatters is advertising; a review that only wounds is cruelty. The honest middle ground is harder to write and far more valuable to read.
Reviewers also watch for integrity. Did the company create its own work, or did it quietly borrow someone else's? Plagiarism on stage is as repugnant as plagiarism on paper, and experienced critics can usually detect it, because borrowed emotion rarely fits its new owner. The productions that audiences remember are almost never the richest or the most elaborate. They are the ones in which every choice, from the humblest prop to the final bow, tells the same truthful story.
As you read this unit's story about a drama competition, keep this passage in mind. Notice who does the invisible work, what happens when a vital prop disappears, and how a team's preparation shows itself in a crisis. Then, when you write your own performance review later in the unit, you will know exactly where to look and exactly what a fair judgement sounds like.

readings.title: The Curtain Never Lies, Part 1: The Competition
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Kampala's Youth Performing Arts Centre pulsed with anticipation. Rows of seats were filling under chandeliers shaped like butterflies. The regional finals were tonight, and schools from across East Africa had sent their best.
In the velvet-draped dressing room, the students from Hillcrest Academy moved with practised energy. Among them was Rohan, tall and focused, adjusting a homemade collar for his lead costume. His fingers were deft, his face calm. He had been mustering the courage to direct his own play for over a year, and now the moment had finally materialized.
Beside him, Imani painted on freckles. "Do you think the crowd will get our theme?" she asked.
"Only if we render it clearly," Rohan replied. He paused. "Do you know what 'render' really means in theatre terms?"
She grinned. "To perform, to evoke, to cause something to be real. I have been paying attention."
Their piece, The Last Contortion, followed a young dancer who faked injuries to manipulate her team. It was meant as a metaphor for artistic honesty.
"What a formidable concept," their literature teacher, Ms Dina, had said when they first proposed it. "But risky."
Risk was the point. Rohan had watched too many competition pieces play safe, and he believed an audience could always tell when a team was merely decorating a stage rather than saying something. Ms Dina had agreed to supervise the production on one condition: whatever happened, the work had to stay honest.
Backstage, Rohan noticed another team, a sleek group from a private school in Nairobi. Their props gleamed. Their costumes shimmered.
"That is Horizon East," someone whispered. "They are notorious for dramatic openings. And drama off-stage too."
Indeed, Horizon East had a reputation. Last year, they had been accused of sabotaging another team's lighting script.
Rohan kept his distance. But later, when he returned to the wings after a break, he found one of their costume bags half-open near his own.
Suspicious, he quickly checked his team's prop trunk.
Gone.
The final scene's concoction, a symbolic mask torn between comedy and tragedy, was missing.
"What happened?" Imani asked, seeing his frozen expression.
Rohan's voice dropped. "The mask is gone."
He went straight to the organiser's desk. "Someone has taken one of our props. It is central to our climax."
A tall woman with a clipboard looked up. "We cannot delay the show, but I will ask around."
Imani pulled him aside. "Do not let this cause havoc in your head. We can still perform."
Rohan stared ahead. "Without the mask, the ending loses weight."
"Then improvise. Your story matters more than a mask."
He inhaled deeply. "You are right. Let us get ready."
In the corridor, the Hillcrest cast formed their usual circle. They breathed in together, held the silence for three counts, and let it go. "Whatever tonight brings," Rohan said quietly, "we tell the story we came to tell."
They stepped onstage. Lights hit. Music began.
Rendered spotlight-blind, Rohan moved through the blocking. Each line hit its mark. The audience leaned in.
Until the climax.
Where the mask should have been, Imani held up a cloth scrap.
The air wallowed in tension.
Rohan hesitated, then stepped forward and tore the cloth into two halves, holding one to each side of his face.
"Comedy or tragedy," he cried, "we make the mask we wear!"
The crowd gasped. Some stood. Applause thundered.
Backstage afterwards, nobody spoke for a long moment. Then the whole cast collapsed into laughter and relief, hugging one another between the racks of borrowed costumes. The mask was still missing; somehow, it no longer mattered.

readings.title: The Curtain Never Lies, Part 2: After the Curtain Falls
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Backstage, Horizon East's leader passed by.
"What a save," she smirked.
"Did you take it?" Rohan asked.
She shrugged. "Could you prove it?"
He glared. "No. But your behaviour was repugnant."
Later, Imani approached him. "You handled that better than I ever could."
He smiled, exhausted. "Honestly, I wanted to charge headlong into their dressing room."
"But you did not. You performed."
"Do you think we will win?"
"I do not know," she said. "But what a performance!"
Judging took two hours. Back in the holding room, they sat in quiet tension. One boy meandered in loops near the window. Another girl rubbed her temples.
The announcer returned. "Third place: Horizon East."
A murmur.
"Second place: Lakeview High."
A pause.
"And the winner of this year's regional youth drama finals: Hillcrest Academy!"
Cheers erupted. Rohan sat stunned. Imani hugged him.
"What an impulsive moment you had," she teased. "And it saved the show."
Weeks later, a judge's email materialized in Rohan's inbox: "You reminded us all why theatre matters, because even when stripped of perfection, it reveals truth."
Rohan smiled. That night, he wrote in his journal: "I nearly gave in to fear. I almost let them sully the work we had built. But we stood tall. Rendered vulnerable, we became stronger."
He read the sentence back twice, wondering when he had started to believe it. The trophy sat on the shelf above his desk, but the email felt heavier than the silverware. Anyone could hold a cup; not everyone could say the curtain had shown an audience something true.
After the competition, Hillcrest Academy was invited to perform the piece again, this time at the Kampala National Theatre. It was a chance to rebuild the show with all the original props and polish every moment.
They had only ten days to prepare, and the process was gruelling. Lights had to be adjusted. The musical cues had to be timed perfectly. Even the transitions between scenes were rehearsed until their feet ached. The choreographer rebuilt the opening sequence three times before she was satisfied, and the youngest cast member learned to reset the props in under a minute.
Rohan noticed how fatigue tested everyone. Some team members grew aloof. Tempers rose. There were disagreements about lines, costumes and entrances. One night, a heated argument broke out over whether a side character should speak or mime.
"I just want it to be accurate," one actor insisted. "We need to preserve what worked."
"But sometimes art evolves," Rohan said, trying to mediate. "We can adjust. The moment will tell us."
Despite the pressure, the team bonded in new ways. They took turns fending off stress with dance breaks and storytelling circles. They joked about their first performance, about how Rohan had almost cried backstage.
On the eve of the show, Ms Dina visited during their final rehearsal. "You have grown," she said after the run. "Not just as a performer. As a leader."
Opening night arrived. The theatre was full. As the curtain rose, Rohan stepped onstage with his ensemble. This time, every prop was in place. But more importantly, their integrity was intact.
The performance flowed with grace and fire. When the mask finally appeared in the final scene, the crowd gasped as though seeing a ghost return.
"What a story," someone whispered aloud. "What a choice."
And when the play ended, the applause was long, loud, and real.

readings.title: The Curtain Never Lies, Part 3: Beyond Borders
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
After their second performance, the cast was approached by two international festival coordinators. One was from Johannesburg's Youth Vision Festival, and the other represented the Nairobi Dramatic Society.
"Would it be too bold," the man from Johannesburg asked politely, "if we invited you to present your play at our July showcase?"
The students were stunned. Rohan blinked, unsure what to say. He glanced at Ms Dina, who nodded gently.
"Yes," Rohan replied. "It would be an honour."
The following weeks were filled with planning and preparation. New scripts were printed. Costumes were adjusted. They practised not only the performance but also how to speak in interviews, how to answer questions from international press, and how to carry themselves in front of strangers.
Rohan found himself reflecting more deeply on what their play had meant, not just to the audience, but to himself. He realised how it mirrored the journey they had all taken: learning to confront insecurity, to resist dishonesty, and to find courage in vulnerability.
At the Johannesburg showcase, Hillcrest Academy performed before a thousand people. The applause that night was thunderous, but what meant more to Rohan was a conversation with a young boy who approached him after the show.
"That play made me cry," the boy said. "Because I lie sometimes too. But I do not want to anymore."
That night, sitting alone on the edge of the performance tent, Rohan scribbled in his notebook: "This is what theatre does. It reflects us, so we can see what to change. And sometimes, it reflects what we already are. Just hidden."
Back home in Kampala, their return was quiet. No parades. Just school as usual. But something had shifted. Teachers gave them respectful nods. Younger students began writing plays of their own.
One Friday, Ms Dina held a lunchtime seminar on ethics in performance, and Rohan was asked to co-lead it.
"What is the most important thing a young artist should remember?" she asked.
Rohan paused. Then he answered, "Do not just ask what you want to say. Ask what your story does to people."

comprehension.question: According to the passage, where does the word 'music' come from, and what did it originally mean?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It comes from the ancient Greek word 'mousike', meaning 'art of the Muses', the figures of inspiration in Greek mythology; the Arabic word 'musiqa' grew from the same root.
comprehension.explanation: A retrieval question: the learner locates the etymology paragraph and reports both the Greek origin and the shared root with 'musiqa'.

comprehension.question: The writer claims music delivers its message without translation. Which two examples in the passage involve listeners who share no common words with the music?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The lullaby that calms a baby who understands no words at all, and the stadium chant that unites thousands of strangers who may share no mother tongue.
comprehension.explanation: Evidence selection: the learner must pick the two examples that specifically remove shared language, not the film-score example.

comprehension.question: What does the passage say a director does with the blocking, and how do her questions change the actors' work in early rehearsals?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She plans the blocking as a map of every actor's movement across the stage, and by asking questions about each character she helps actors stop reciting and start becoming their roles.
comprehension.explanation: A two-part retrieval and inference question about the director's craft as described in the second paragraph.

comprehension.question: According to the passage, what four things does a useful performance review do?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It describes precisely what happened on stage, praises specific strengths with evidence, criticises constructively with suggestions, and weighs both sides to give a fair recommendation.
comprehension.explanation: Structure retrieval: the four functions of a review are listed in sequence in the fifth paragraph and feed directly into the unit's writing project.

comprehension.question: What has Rohan been doing for over a year, and which sentence in the passage tells you so?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He has been mustering the courage to direct his own play; the passage says he 'had been mustering the courage to direct his own play for over a year'.
comprehension.explanation: This checks quotation skills and highlights the unit's Present Perfect Continuous focus inside the narrative itself.

comprehension.question: Describe The Last Contortion. What is the play about, and how does Ms Dina react when the students first propose it?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It follows a young dancer who fakes injuries to manipulate her team and is meant as a metaphor for artistic honesty; Ms Dina calls it a formidable concept but warns that it is risky.
comprehension.explanation: Retrieval plus viewpoint: the learner summarises the play-within-the-story and quotes the teacher's double-edged reaction.

comprehension.question: What does Rohan find missing from the prop trunk, and how does he turn the loss into the strongest moment of the show?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The symbolic mask, torn between comedy and tragedy, is missing; at the climax he tears a cloth scrap into two halves, holds one to each side of his face and cries, 'Comedy or tragedy, we make the mask we wear!'
comprehension.explanation: Sequence and interpretation: the learner links the backstage discovery to the improvised climax that wins over the audience.

comprehension.question: How does Imani steady Rohan after the discovery backstage? Quote the two pieces of advice she gives him.
comprehension.correctAnswer: She tells him, 'Do not let this cause havoc in your head. We can still perform,' and then urges him, 'Then improvise. Your story matters more than a mask.'
comprehension.explanation: Character and quotation: Imani's calm advice is the turning point that lets the performance go ahead.

comprehension.question: How does Rohan handle the confrontation with Horizon East's leader, and what single word does he use to judge her behaviour?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He asks her directly whether she took the mask, admits he cannot prove it, and calls her behaviour repugnant, even though he privately wanted to charge headlong into their dressing room.
comprehension.explanation: Inference with evidence: the learner contrasts Rohan's controlled words with the angry impulse he confesses to Imani afterwards.

comprehension.question: What result does the announcer declare, and what message does the judge's email deliver weeks later?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Horizon East takes third place, Lakeview High second, and Hillcrest Academy wins; the judge's email says the team reminded everyone why theatre matters, because even stripped of perfection it reveals truth.
comprehension.explanation: Retrieval across two scenes: the placings in the holding room and the email that arrives weeks afterwards.

comprehension.question: What pressures test the team during the ten days before the National Theatre performance, and how do they cope with them?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The gruelling schedule of adjusting lights, timing musical cues and rehearsing transitions leaves members aloof and short-tempered, with arguments over lines and costumes, but they cope by fending off stress with dance breaks and storytelling circles.
comprehension.explanation: Synthesis within one passage: the learner gathers the strains of the rebuild and the team's own remedies.

comprehension.question: What does the young boy in Johannesburg confess to Rohan, and how does Rohan's notebook entry that night explain what the title 'The Curtain Never Lies' means?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The boy says the play made him cry because he lies sometimes too but does not want to anymore; Rohan writes that theatre reflects us so we can see what to change, meaning the stage always shows the truth about the people on it and in front of it.
comprehension.explanation: Evaluation: the learner connects one audience member's honesty to the story's moral and the meaning of its title.

grammar.title: Present Perfect Continuous
grammar.explanation: The Present Perfect Continuous describes actions that began in the past and are still running now, or that have only just stopped and left visible evidence, as when paint-stained hands tell you someone has been painting. It is built with has or have, then been, then the -ing form of the verb, and it puts the spotlight on how long an activity has lasted rather than on whether it finished.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Form: subject + has/have + been + verb-ing. Use has been with he, she and it: 'She has been mustering the courage to perform.' Use have been with I, you, we and they: 'They have been rehearsing since morning.'
Negative: 'She has not been practising enough this week.' Question: 'Have they been rehearsing all day?' — 'Yes, they have.'
Use it for actions still continuing ('I have been studying English for three years'), recent actions with visible results ('She has been crying — her eyes are red'), the duration of ongoing activity ('They have been waiting for twenty minutes') and repeated actions over a period ('He has been performing in school plays since Year 6').
Key time words: for + a period ('for five years'), since + a starting point ('since Monday'), all day or all week ('She has been composing music all day'), how long ('How long have you been learning the drums?') and lately or recently ('I have been feeling more confident lately').
Compare it with the Present Perfect Simple: the continuous form stresses the process ('I have been reading this book all week'), while the simple form stresses the result ('I have read three chapters').
grammar.commonMistake: Four slips recur with this tense: dropping 'been' ('She has mustering the courage'), pairing the wrong form of 'have' ('They has been studying'), keeping the base verb instead of the -ing form ('She has been muster the courage'), and stretching the tense onto stative verbs — say 'I have known him for years', never 'I have been knowing him'.
grammar.memoryTip: Think of it as the 'how long' tense: if the question 'How long have you been doing this?' fits naturally, the Present Perfect Continuous is the form you want.
grammar.practice:
Part A — complete each sentence with the Present Perfect Continuous: 1) I ______ (play) the guitar for three hours. 2) He ______ (learn) to dance since last summer. 3) They ______ (wait) for the bus for twenty minutes. 4) She ______ (muster) the courage to perform all week. 5) We ______ (rehearse) this scene since Monday. 6) How long ______ you ______ (practise) the piano? Part B — now use the story sentences: 1) Rohan ______ (direct) his own play for over a year. 2) The students ______ (rehearse) every evening since September. 3) She ______ (paint) stage decorations all morning; her hands are covered in colour. 4) How long ______ you ______ (wait) for the judges to announce the results? 5) We ______ (practise) this scene for two hours and we are still not satisfied. 6) He ______ (compose) music since he was twelve years old. 7) They ______ (argue) about the costumes all afternoon. 8) Imani ______ (learn) to play the oud for three months now.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: 1) I have been playing the guitar for three hours. 2) He has been learning to dance since last summer. 3) They have been waiting for the bus for twenty minutes. 4) She has been mustering the courage to perform all week. 5) We have been rehearsing this scene since Monday. 6) How long have you been practising the piano?
Part B: 1) Rohan has been directing his own play for over a year. 2) The students have been rehearsing every evening since September. 3) She has been painting stage decorations all morning; her hands are covered in colour. 4) How long have you been waiting for the judges to announce the results? 5) We have been practising this scene for two hours and we are still not satisfied. 6) He has been composing music since he was twelve years old. 7) They have been arguing about the costumes all afternoon. 8) Imani has been learning to play the oud for three months now.

grammar.title: Participle Clauses
grammar.explanation: A participle clause lets you fold two sentences into one elegant line: instead of 'She was rendered breathless by the performance. She collapsed backstage,' you write 'Rendered breathless, she collapsed backstage.' Because the clause borrows its subject from the main clause, it trims repetition and gives your writing a more sophisticated rhythm.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Present participles end in -ing (running, feeling, performing); past participles end in -ed or take irregular forms (excited, rendered, hidden, torn); perfect participles use having + past participle (having rehearsed).
To build one: take the main clause ('She collapsed backstage'), take the extra information ('She was rendered breathless'), strip the subject and auxiliary ('Rendered breathless'), then combine: 'Rendered breathless, she collapsed backstage.'
Examples from the unit: 'Rendered spotlight-blind, Rohan moved through the blocking' (state); 'Feeling tired, he went to bed early' (reason); 'Excited about the showcase, she packed her costume with care' (emotion); 'Having rehearsed all day, they were exhausted by evening' (earlier action).
Participle clauses can signal reason ('Worried about the exam, he studied late into the night'), time ('Arriving at the theatre, she noticed the long queue'), result ('The power went out, plunging the stage into darkness') and manner ('He left the stage, bowing to the audience').
One firm rule: the subject of the participle clause must match the subject of the main clause. 'Feeling hungry, the pizza was eaten' claims the pizza felt hungry; write 'Feeling hungry, he ate the pizza.'
grammar.commonMistake: The classic error is the dangling participle, where the subjects do not match: 'Walking to the theatre, the rain started' makes the rain do the walking — say 'Walking to the theatre, she got caught in the rain.' Learners also swap participle forms: a person is 'excited' by a show, while the show itself is 'exciting'.
grammar.memoryTip: Before the comma, ask 'who is doing this?' — if the answer is not the subject that follows the comma, the participle is dangling and the sentence needs rebuilding.
grammar.practice:
Part A — combine each pair with a participle clause: 1) She was excited by the news. She jumped up and down. 2) He was tired from running. He sat down on the grass. 3) She was surprised by the gift. She could not stop smiling. 4) He was inspired by the story. He began writing his own play. 5) They were determined to succeed. They rehearsed every evening. Part B — now the unit versions: 1) She was exhausted from rehearsal. She fell asleep on the bus home. 2) He was inspired by the music. He decided to learn the guitar. 3) They were determined to win. They practised every single day. 4) She was surprised by the standing ovation. She could not stop smiling. 5) He was frustrated by the missing prop. He almost cancelled the show.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: 1) Excited by the news, she jumped up and down. 2) Tired from running, he sat down on the grass. 3) Surprised by the gift, she could not stop smiling. 4) Inspired by the story, he began writing his own play. 5) Determined to succeed, they rehearsed every evening.
Part B: 1) Exhausted from rehearsal, she fell asleep on the bus home. 2) Inspired by the music, he decided to learn the guitar. 3) Determined to win, they practised every single day. 4) Surprised by the standing ovation, she could not stop smiling. 5) Frustrated by the missing prop, he almost cancelled the show.
Self-check tip: the person named right after the comma must be the one doing the feeling/action described in the participle clause (no dangling participles).

grammar.title: What Clauses for Exclamations
grammar.explanation: Exclamations built with 'what' turn a plain observation into a burst of feeling: 'What a formidable concept!' says far more than 'That concept is formidable.' The story reaches for this structure at its most emotional moments, and learning it will make your own speech and writing more expressive.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
With a singular countable noun the pattern is What + a / an + adjective + noun: 'What a formidable performance!', 'What an impulsive act!', 'What a wonderful surprise!'
With plural or uncountable nouns, drop the article: 'What talented musicians!' (plural), 'What beautiful music!' (uncountable), 'What deft fingers!' (plural).
'What' and 'how' behave differently: 'what' takes a noun ('What a beautiful song!') while 'how' takes an adjective alone ('How beautiful!').
Three mistakes to avoid: never open a noun exclamation with 'how' ('How a beautiful day!' should be 'What a beautiful day!'); never drop the adjective ('What dog!' should be 'What a cute dog!'); and never keep the article before a plural ('What a talented musicians!' should be 'What talented musicians!').
grammar.commonMistake: The most frequent slip is keeping 'a' where no article belongs: plurals and uncountables take none, so it is 'What talented musicians!' and 'What beautiful music!', never 'What a talented musicians!' Check the noun before you choose the opener.
grammar.memoryTip: Hear something amazing, then build outwards: What + a or an + adjective + noun — and if the noun is plural or uncountable, the little article simply disappears.
grammar.practice:
Part A — build an exclamation with a fitting adjective and noun for each situation: 1) a very impressive concert 2) a surprising ending to a play 3) a group of very skilled dancers 4) an elaborate mask 5) deeply moving music. Part B — turn each plain sentence into a what-clause exclamation: 1) The costume was beautiful. 2) The save was amazing. 3) The concept was formidable. 4) The musicians were talented. 5) The decision was impulsive. Part C — write two exclamations of your own about a performance you have seen, one with a singular noun and one with a plural noun.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A (model answers — your own adjective choice is fine as long as the article rule is followed): 1) What an impressive concert! 2) What a surprising ending! 3) What skilled dancers! (plural noun, so no article) 4) What an elaborate mask! 5) What moving music! (uncountable noun, so no article)
Part B: 1) What a beautiful costume! 2) What an amazing save! 3) What a formidable concept! 4) What talented musicians! (plural, no article) 5) What an impulsive decision!
Part C is open-ended (your own two exclamations about a performance). Self-check instead of a fixed answer: does the singular-noun sentence follow What + a/an + adjective + noun (e.g. "What a thrilling performance!"), does the plural-noun sentence drop the article (e.g. "What talented singers!"), and does each sentence end with an exclamation mark rather than a full stop?

grammar.title: Polite Question Structures
grammar.explanation: Polite question structures let you ask for help, information or favours while showing respect for the listener's time and feelings. They matter most in formal situations and with people you have just met, and the story models them twice: 'Do you know what render really means in theatre terms?' and 'Would it be too bold if we invited you to present your play?'
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Five reliable openers: 'Could you...?' ('Could you please explain that scene again?'); 'Would you mind...?' followed by verb-ing ('Would you mind passing the script?'); 'Do you know...?' with an embedded question ('Do you know where the theatre is?'); 'Would you be able to...?' ('Would you be able to attend the rehearsal tomorrow?'); and the very formal 'I was wondering if...' ('I was wondering if you could give me some feedback on my performance.').
The key rule is embedded word order: inside a polite frame, the question flips to statement order. 'What time does the show start?' becomes 'Do you know what time the show starts?', and 'Where is the dressing room?' becomes 'Could you tell me where the dressing room is?'
Adding 'please' raises the politeness another step: 'Could you please help me with my lines?'
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often keep question word order inside the polite frame — 'Do you know what does meander mean?' — when the embedded clause needs statement order: 'Do you know what meander means?' A second slip is closing a polite request with a full stop; it is still a question, so it still ends with a question mark.
grammar.memoryTip: Politeness folds the question inside a wrapper, and the wrapper takes the question mark — so inside the wrapper, the words relax into plain statement order.
grammar.practice:
Part A — rewrite each direct question politely, using the opener in brackets: 1) What does 'sabotage' mean? (Do you know...) 2) Can you help me fix this costume? (Would you mind...) 3) Where is the nearest exit? (Could you tell me...) 4) Will you attend the rehearsal tomorrow? (Would you be able to...) 5) What time does the show start? (Do you happen to know...) Part B — the same again with new content: 1) What does 'meander' mean? (Do you know...) 2) Can you explain the scene again? (Would you mind...) 3) Where is the rehearsal room? (Could you tell me...) 4) Will you help me with my costume? (Would you be able to...) 5) What time does the performance start? (Do you happen to know...) Part C — write two polite questions you could ask a visiting director about their work.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: 1) Do you know what 'sabotage' means? 2) Would you mind helping me fix this costume? 3) Could you tell me where the nearest exit is? 4) Would you be able to attend the rehearsal tomorrow? 5) Do you happen to know what time the show starts?
Part B: 1) Do you know what 'meander' means? 2) Would you mind explaining the scene again? 3) Could you tell me where the rehearsal room is? 4) Would you be able to help me with my costume? 5) Do you happen to know what time the performance starts?
Part C is open-ended (your own two polite questions for a visiting director). Self-check instead of a fixed answer: does each question use one of the polite openers from ruleAndExamples (Could you..., Would you mind..., Do you know..., Would you be able to..., I was wondering if...), does the embedded clause stay in statement word order (e.g. "what he likes", not "what does he like"), and does the sentence still end with a question mark?

grammar.title: Reported Speech
grammar.explanation: Reported speech carries another person's words into your own sentence without quotation marks: 'He said, I like music' becomes 'He said that he liked music.' It is the backbone of summaries, journalism and storytelling, because it lets you weave conversations smoothly into prose.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Four changes happen at once. Remove the quotation marks and add 'that' after the reporting verb. Shift the tense one step back: present simple to past simple, present continuous to past continuous, present perfect to past perfect, past simple to past perfect, will to would, can to could. Change the pronouns: I becomes he or she, we becomes they, my becomes his or her. Change time and place words: today becomes that day, tomorrow becomes the next day, now becomes then, here becomes there.
Examples: Rohan said, 'The performance caused havoc' becomes Rohan said that the performance had caused havoc. Imani said, 'I am tired of giving in' becomes Imani said that she was tired of giving in. The teacher told the students, 'You will perform tomorrow' becomes the teacher told the students that they would perform the next day.
Questions change shape too. Yes-or-no questions take if or whether: 'Did you save the props?' becomes He asked if she had saved the props. Wh- questions keep their question word but take statement order and lose the question mark: 'Where did you hide the mask?' becomes He asked where she had hidden the mask.
Choose reporting verbs precisely: said is neutral; told always names a listener; explained gives reasons; announced makes a public statement; asked reports a question; warned signals danger: 'She warned that cheating was repugnant.'
grammar.commonMistake: The two habits to break are leaving the tense unshifted — 'He said that he will come' needs 'He said that he would come' — and forgetting to swap the pronoun when reporting someone else's words, which turns 'She said that she was tired' into the very different 'She said that I was tired.'
grammar.memoryTip: Picture reported speech as one step back in time and one step away in person: tenses step back, while pronouns and time words step away from the original speaker.
grammar.practice:
Part A — change each sentence to reported speech: 1) Rohan said, 'I have been directing this play for over a year.' 2) Imani told him, 'Do not let this cause havoc in your head.' 3) The judge said, 'This is the most original performance we have seen today.' 4) The boy asked Rohan, 'Will you perform here again?' Part B — continue with these: 1) Imani told him, 'Your story matters more than a mask.' 2) The teacher announced, 'We will perform at the National Theatre next month.' 3) The boy in Johannesburg said, 'That play made me cry.' Part C — report two things a family member said to you this week, shifting tense, pronouns and time words carefully.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: 1) Rohan said that he had been directing that play for over a year. 2) Imani told him not to let that cause havoc in his head. 3) The judge said that that was the most original performance they had seen that day. 4) The boy asked Rohan if he would perform there again.
Note on Part A, item 2: this line reports a command, not a statement or a yes/no question, so it does not fit the statement/question patterns in ruleAndExamples above. The standard reported-speech convention for commands is "told + object + (not) + to-infinitive" — e.g. "Do this" becomes "told him to do it," and "Don't do this" becomes "told him not to do it," which is how the answer above was built.
Part B: 1) Imani told him that his story mattered more than a mask. 2) The teacher announced that they would perform at the National Theatre the following month. 3) The boy in Johannesburg said that that play had made him cry.
Part C is open-ended (report two things a family member said to you this week). grammar.title: Reflexive Pronouns
grammar.explanation: Reflexive pronouns step in when the subject and the object of a sentence are the same person or thing: 'She expressed herself through the performance.' Without them, sentences about self-directed actions turn ambiguous or simply break down.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Each subject pronoun owns a reflexive partner: I takes myself; you takes yourself; he takes himself; she takes herself; it takes itself; we takes ourselves; plural you takes yourselves; they takes themselves.
Place the reflexive pronoun after the verb or at the end of the sentence: 'She dressed herself in the costume', 'We enjoyed ourselves at the performance', 'He taught himself how to play the guitar', 'They prepared themselves for the big show.'
Reflexives also add emphasis: 'Rohan himself directed the entire play' insists that he did it personally, and 'I will do it myself' means without anyone's help.
grammar.commonMistake: Match the reflexive to its subject — 'She enjoyed himself at the party' pairs the wrong people, so it must be 'She enjoyed herself at the party.' The other trap is dropping the pronoun where the meaning needs it: 'He taught to play the guitar' is incomplete without 'himself'.
grammar.memoryTip: A reflexive pronoun works like a mirror: whatever the subject does bounces straight back to the subject, so both ends of the sentence must show the same face.
grammar.practice:
Part A — complete each sentence with the correct reflexive pronoun: 1) She expressed ______ through a gaudy costume. 2) I taught ______ how to play the oud. 3) They prepared ______ for the big performance. 4) He looked at ______ in the mirror before going on stage. 5) We enjoyed ______ at the drama festival. 6) You should believe in ______. Part B — three more from the unit: 1) He taught ______ how to play the drums by watching videos online. 2) We pushed ______ to rehearse harder during the final week. 3) I reminded ______ to stay calm before walking onto the stage. Part C — mixed review: write one original sentence for each instruction, using unit vocabulary where you can: 1) the Present Perfect Continuous about something you have been doing recently 2) a participle clause describing a reaction to a performance 3) a what-clause exclamation of admiration 4) a polite question about someone's favourite music 5) reported speech about something a friend told you about a concert 6) a reflexive pronoun about something you did by yourself.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: 1) She expressed herself through a gaudy costume. 2) I taught myself how to play the oud. 3) They prepared themselves for the big performance. 4) He looked at himself in the mirror before going on stage. 5) We enjoyed ourselves at the drama festival. 6) You should believe in yourself.
Part B: 1) He taught himself how to play the drums by watching videos online. 2) We pushed ourselves to rehearse harder during the final week. 3) I reminded myself to stay calm before walking onto the stage.
Part C is open-ended (six original sentences, one per instruction). Self-check with model examples instead of a fixed answer: (1) Present Perfect Continuous about something recent, e.g. "I have been practising the piano every day this week." (2) a participle clause describing a reaction, e.g. "Amazed by the finale, I clapped for a full minute." (3) a what-clause exclamation of admiration, e.g. "What a stunning performance!" (4) a polite question about a favourite kind of music, e.g. "Could you tell me what kind of music you enjoy most?" (5) reported speech about something a friend told you, e.g. "My friend said that the concert had been the best she had ever seen." (6) a reflexive pronoun about something done alone, e.g. "I taught myself to read music."

speaking.title: Speaking 1: Role-Play Interview with a Performer
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
One of you is a journalist; the other is a young performer who has just won the regional drama final. The journalist prepares at least five questions about the performance, the preparation and the emotions involved, using polite structures: 'Could you tell us about...?', 'Would you mind explaining...?', 'Do you know what inspired...?' The performer answers in character, as Rohan, Imani or an invented cast member, using unit vocabulary and the Present Perfect Continuous: 'I have been rehearsing for months', 'We have been working on this play since September.'
Perform the interview for your family, your classmates or your AI tutor with an adult nearby, and record it if possible. Afterwards, the journalist writes a four- to five-sentence summary in reported speech: 'Rohan explained that he had been directing his own play for over a year. He added that the missing prop had made the team feel vulnerable.'
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Play a journalist and interview me as a performer from 'The Curtain Never Lies'; push me to answer with the Present Perfect Continuous, then check my reported-speech summary.

speaking.title: Speaking 2: Group Discussion — Music Across Cultures
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Discuss these questions with a partner, a group, your family or your AI tutor, speaking for one to two minutes on each. Use opinion phrases such as 'I believe that...', 'In my view...' and 'It seems to me that...', and support every view with an example.
1) What kinds of music are popular in your community, and why do people enjoy them? 2) Describe a time when music or a performance brought people together. 3) The story claims that art only matters when it is honest; do you agree? 4) Can music communicate things that language cannot? 5) How can the performing arts build confidence, teamwork and creativity? 6) Imani says, 'Your story matters more than a mask.' What does she mean, and is she right? 7) If you had been in Rohan's position when the mask disappeared, would you have confronted Horizon East or focused on performing?
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Host a discussion with me about music across cultures; challenge my opinions politely and ask me for an example every time I make a claim.

speaking.title: Speaking 3: Dramatic Reading
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Choose one of the most dramatic scenes from 'The Curtain Never Lies' and perform it as a dramatic reading, alone or with a partner. Change your tone for different characters, pause at the tensest moments, and speak clearly enough for a listener to follow the whole story.
Suggested scenes: the moment Rohan discovers the missing mask and Imani steadies him; the climax when Rohan improvises with the torn cloth; the confrontation with Horizon East's leader after the show; Rohan's conversation with the young boy in Johannesburg.
Afterwards, ask your audience or your AI tutor which moment landed hardest, which emotions came through most clearly, and what one thing you could improve.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Listen to my dramatic reading of a scene from 'The Curtain Never Lies' and give me feedback on pace, tone changes between characters and dramatic pauses.

speaking.title: Speaking 6: Six-Minute Unit Argument
speaking.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Plan and record a six-minute argument on this claim: the performing arts deserve a central place in school life. Open with a focused statement of your position, then build connected claims with synthesized evidence from the unit — the story's competition, the information texts on performance and reviewing, and your own experience. Evaluate your sources explicitly, present the strongest counterargument fairly, rebut it, and close with purpose.
Develop this into a sustained five- to six-minute response, then answer two follow-up questions from your listener without losing the thread of your argument.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Time my six-minute argument about the performing arts in school life, then ask me two challenging follow-up questions and score my rebuttal.

writing.title: Writing 1: Performance Review
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a review of a live performance, either one you have really attended or Hillcrest Academy's award-winning show from 'The Curtain Never Lies'. If you prefer, write it as the journalist who attended the regional final and witnessed the missing-mask improvisation. Aim for 250 to 350 words.
Structure your review in five paragraphs. Open by stating what the performance was, who performed it, where and when it took place, and your overall impression in one sentence. Summarise the key moments on stage without retelling the whole plot. Describe what worked well, using specific evidence such as convincing acting, moving music or effective set design. Offer constructive criticism, naming anything unclear or uneven and suggesting an improvement. Close with your final opinion, a clear recommendation and a memorable last sentence.
Before you submit, check that you have used at least five unit vocabulary words, the Present Perfect Continuous at least once (for example, 'The cast has been rehearsing for months'), one participle clause (for example, 'Rendered speechless by the finale, the audience rose to their feet') and one what-clause exclamation such as 'What a formidable performance!' Check spelling, punctuation and balance before calling the review finished.
writing.modelText: The strongest reviews sound fair: they quote real moments as evidence, balance praise with precise criticism, and let the reader feel the performance without having attended it.
writing.sentenceStarter: From the moment the curtain rose,
writing.expectedLength: Five cohesive paragraphs of 250 to 350 words
writing.successCriteria: I described the performance precisely; I balanced strengths and improvements with evidence; I used five unit words, the Present Perfect Continuous, a participle clause and a what-clause exclamation; I ended with a clear recommendation
writing.support: Plan one paragraph per section of the structure before drafting, and collect three specific moments from the show to use as evidence.
writing.extension: Write a second, shorter review of the same show for a different audience, such as a sixty-word social media post, and compare the choices each format forced.

writing.title: Writing 2: Persuasive Speech — Why the Arts Matter
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Imagine your school assembly has asked you to argue that the performing arts deserve time, space and support in education. Write a persuasive speech of 200 to 300 words.
Open with a hook: a question, a surprising fact or a short anecdote. State your thesis in one clear sentence. Present three arguments, each supported by an example or fact — you may borrow evidence from this unit, such as how one honest performance in the story changed a young stranger's behaviour. Acknowledge one counterargument, then rebut it. Finish with a summary and a powerful call to action.
Use persuasive phrases such as 'I firmly believe that...', 'The evidence clearly shows that...' and 'Some may argue that..., but in reality...'. Include at least three unit vocabulary words and at least one polite question that draws your audience in.
writing.modelText: A persuasive speech moves in one direction: every paragraph, example and question should push the audience one step closer to agreeing with the call to action.
writing.expectedLength: Five persuasive paragraphs of 200 to 300 words
writing.successCriteria: I hooked the audience and stated a clear thesis; I gave three supported arguments; I acknowledged and rebutted a counterargument; I used three unit words and one polite question; I closed with a call to action
writing.support: Draft the thesis and the call to action first, then build the three arguments that connect them.
writing.extension: Deliver the speech aloud, time it, and revise any sentence you stumbled over — spoken rhythm is part of persuasion.

writing.title: Writing 3: Diary Entry — Imani's Night
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write the diary entry Imani might have written on the night of the regional final, in the first person. How did she feel when the mask disappeared? What went through her mind as Rohan tore the cloth in two? What does she think now that Hillcrest Academy has won? Aim for 100 to 150 words.
Use the Present Perfect Continuous to describe what she has been doing and feeling: 'We have been rehearsing this ending for weeks, and suddenly it was gone.' Keep her voice consistent with the story: calm, loyal and quick-thinking.
writing.modelText: A convincing diary entry sounds private: it records feelings the writer would never say aloud, in the order the night actually unfolded.
writing.expectedLength: Three short diary paragraphs of 100 to 150 words
writing.successCriteria: I wrote in a consistent first-person voice; I covered the discovery, the improvisation and the result; I used the Present Perfect Continuous at least once; I stayed within the word range
writing.support: Reread the two scenes in Part 1 where Imani speaks, and borrow her calm tone.
writing.extension: Write a second entry from the night of the National Theatre performance and show how her confidence has changed.

writing.title: Writing 4: Formal Letter to a Young Fan
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write the letter Rohan sends to the young boy he met after the Johannesburg showcase, thanking him for his honesty and encouraging him to stay truthful. Use formal language, a clear opening and closing, and at least three vocabulary words from this unit — 'vulnerable', 'sully' and 'muster' all fit naturally. Aim for 100 to 150 words.
Remember what the boy admitted: the play made him cry because he lies sometimes too, but he does not want to anymore. Rohan's letter should honour that courage without lecturing.
writing.modelText: A formal letter to a younger reader stays warm but precise: short sentences, no slang, and encouragement grounded in something the reader actually did.
writing.expectedLength: Three formal paragraphs of 100 to 150 words
writing.successCriteria: I used a formal opening and closing; I referred to the boy's own words; I included three unit vocabulary words used accurately; I encouraged without lecturing
writing.support: List the three vocabulary words first and plan one sentence around each of them.
writing.extension: Write the boy's short reply, keeping his younger, simpler voice clearly distinct from Rohan's.

writing.title: Writing 5: What Your Story Does to People
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: At the ethics seminar, Rohan says: 'Do not just ask what you want to say. Ask what your story does to people.' Write one developed paragraph of 80 to 100 words explaining what this advice means for young artists. Consider both halves of the sentence: why is wanting to say something not enough, and what responsibility does an artist take on once an audience is listening? Support your explanation with one moment from the story where a performance visibly changed someone.
writing.modelText: A strong explanation paragraph states the idea in its own words, unpacks it in two or three sentences, and lands on one concrete example.
writing.expectedLength: One developed paragraph of 80 to 100 words
writing.successCriteria: I explained the advice in my own words; I addressed both halves of the quotation; I supported the explanation with one story moment; I stayed within the word range
writing.support: Try completing the frame 'Artists should ask... because audiences...' before drafting.
writing.extension: Apply the advice to a song, film or book you know: what does that story do to its audience?

writing.title: Writing 6: Summary Writing Workshop
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Good summaries keep the main ideas and cut everything else. Follow the seven steps: read carefully; identify the key ideas; combine related ideas with connecting words; remove unnecessary detail; use your own words; keep it concise; review and revise. A summary is usually one-quarter to one-third the length of the original.
Task 1: summarise the Johannesburg showcase scene — the thousand-person audience, the applause and the boy's confession — in two to three sentences.
Task 2: summarise the whole of Part 1 of 'The Curtain Never Lies' in one paragraph of no more than six sentences, covering the competition, the missing mask and the improvised climax. Paraphrase throughout: copying whole sentences from the story is not summarising.
writing.modelText: Model summary: Hillcrest Academy performed to a large audience in Johannesburg, and afterwards a young boy told Rohan the play had made him want to stop lying, which showed the power of honest theatre.
writing.expectedLength: Two summary paragraphs, each significantly shorter than its source
writing.successCriteria: I kept every key idea and cut minor detail; I paraphrased instead of copying; I connected ideas with linking words; both summaries are far shorter than their source passages
writing.support: Underline the who, what, where and why in each passage before writing a word.
writing.extension: Summarise Part 2 in exactly twenty-five words, then decide what the tight limit forced you to drop.
